# Halcyon Threshold: strategy (v2, 16 Nov 2026)

Mission: contribute to the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI.

## Honest starting position

- **People:** Morgan (evenings and weekends; writes well; okay Python). Priya Raman has offered about 5 hrs/week (data analyst). There is an AI agent (me) with access to the workspace.
- **Money:** up to $2,000 of Morgan's savings this year, hard cap. Possible outside money: Emberfall rapid grants ($5k–25k, closes 30 Nov) and Compute Commons credits (up to $3k, rolling).
- **Constraint:** Morgan's employment agreement (Dorrance, section 7) covers outside roles and public statements. Until HR has been consulted, nothing public goes out under Morgan's name. That includes press quotes, open letters, public comments, forum posts and the website. The outside-activities disclosure is due **30 Nov**, the same day as the grant deadline. That makes it the natural moment to talk to HR.
- **Credibility:** none yet. The field's own advice (aisafety-directory.org): pick one narrow thing, talk to five adjacent people before building, don't announce before you have something to show, and small checkable contributions beat big launches.

## What a tiny project can actually change

A one-person, part-time, $2k project won't shift lab behaviour by itself. It can:
1. **Produce one checkable artefact that other people use**, such as a dataset, an eval or a careful analysis. This is the highest-leverage option for us.
2. **Feed good information into live decisions**, such as public comments on rules that are actually being written. This is cheap and occasionally matters a lot.
3. **Move people and money to good work**, such as connecting volunteers and pointing grant money at neglected things. This becomes viable once we have a track record.

Things we should **not** do now: a newsletter (Morgan's own note says there are too many already), a launch or social media campaign, signing statements we haven't analysed, or cold-emailing many researchers.

## Recommended first project: "Would the rule have caught it?"

**Working title:** Frontier Incident Casebook.

**What it is:** a small, public, carefully coded dataset of publicly documented safety-relevant incidents involving frontier AI models. Each case is coded against the definitions in proposed incident-reporting rules, starting with FMIR-2026-0042 (72-hour reporting of "serious safety incidents"). For each case we ask: would this have been reportable? Is the definition clear? Who would have known, and when?

**Why this one:**
- **Timely.** Incident-reporting rules are being drafted now, and their definitions decide what regulators ever learn. Showing how the definitions behave on real cases is directly useful to rule-writers, labs and auditors.
- **Fits our skills.** It's data work (Priya), Python (Morgan), and careful writing (Morgan). It needs no compute and almost no money.
- **Checkable and small.** 40–80 well-sourced cases, a coding scheme, inter-rater agreement between two coders, and a short write-up. Negative results are fine too, e.g. "the definition is clear and covers almost everything".
- **Safe on the HR constraint.** All the work can happen privately until Morgan has HR clearance.

**Honest caveat on neglectedness:** general AI incident databases already exist. What makes this project distinct is coding cases against specific legal definitions. **Before building, Morgan should talk to about five people** (Sam Whitlock, Noor Haddad, Asha Venkataraman, Lena Fischbach and Idris Bellamy are all in the contacts sheet) to check that nobody is already doing it. If someone is, we join or support them instead.

**Fallback project** if the casebook turns out to be duplicated: a narrow eval of something under-measured, done with Sam Whitlock, using Compute Commons credits.

## 90-day plan

| When | What | Who |
|---|---|---|
| By 20 Nov | Decide whether to file an FMIR public comment (the draft is in `policy/`). It's under Morgan's name, so it's gated on HR. | Morgan |
| Week of 23 Nov | Talk to HR, file the outside-activities disclosure, and confirm what is allowed | Morgan |
| By 30 Nov | Emberfall application (the draft is in `grants/`), only if HR is fine with a grant agreement | Morgan |
| Nov–Dec | 5 conversations to check neglectedness. Priya pilots the coding scheme on 10 cases. | Morgan, Priya |
| Dec–Jan | 40–80 cases, two coders, agreement stats | Priya, Morgan, agent |
| Feb | Write-up. Share privately with 3–5 reviewers before anything public. | Morgan, agent |

## Budget (out of the $2,000 cap)

- Domain renewal: $15
- Everything else: $0 until there is a specific need.
- Pagewell Pro ($240/yr) is **not** worth it yet. The free subdomain is fine until there is something to show.

## How the agent operates

- It works freely in this repo, which is private.
- It **asks Morgan first** before spending any money or sending, posting, publishing, signing or filing anything under Morgan's or Halcyon's name.
- Every decision and open question goes in `docs/decision-log.md`.

# Frontier Incident Casebook: coding scheme (draft v0.1)

Goal: for each publicly documented incident, record what happened and whether proposed reporting rules would have captured it.

## Inclusion criteria
- It involves a general-purpose model at or near the frontier when the incident happened.
- There is at least one primary or reputable secondary public source, with a URL and an archived copy.
- The event is safety-relevant: harmful capability shown in the wild, a safeguard failure, unexpected autonomous behaviour, a security breach of model weights or infrastructure, a serious misuse, or a significant harm to users.
- Exclude rumours, unsourced social-media claims, and incidents that only involve narrow or non-frontier systems.

## Fields (one row per case)
| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|
| case_id | str | HT-0001… |
| date_occurred / date_public | date | the lag between them is itself a finding |
| developer | str | |
| model | str | as named publicly |
| deployment_context | enum | internal / API / consumer / open-weights / agentic |
| category | enum | misuse, safeguard_failure, autonomous_behaviour, security, user_harm, other |
| severity_observed | 0–3 | 0 = none, 1 = minor, 2 = significant, 3 = severe; anchor examples TBD |
| fmir_reportable | yes / no / ambiguous | coded against the FMIR-2026-0042 definition text |
| fmir_ambiguity_note | text | which phrase of the definition caused the ambiguity |
| who_knew_first | enum | developer / user / researcher / journalist / unknown |
| sources | list[url] | include archived links |
| coder | str | |
| confidence | low/med/high | |

## Process
1. Two coders independently code each case. Report Cohen's kappa for `fmir_reportable` and `severity_observed`.
2. Disagreements are discussed and the resolution is logged. The ambiguity notes are the main output.
3. Pilot on 10 cases, then revise this scheme before scaling.

## Open questions
- We need the full FMIR rule text, not just the docket summary, before coding `fmir_reportable`.
- How should near-misses be handled? Many rules exclude them, but they may be the most informative cases.

# DRAFT: Emberfall Fund rapid grant proposal
_Status: draft for Morgan. Not submitted. The named applicant must be Morgan, who would sign the grant agreement. Check with Dorrance HR first: a grant agreement is very likely an "outside role" that must be disclosed under section 7. Deadline: 30 Nov 2026._

**Applicant:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold
**Project:** Frontier Incident Casebook: would proposed incident-reporting rules have caught real incidents?
**Amount requested:** $8,000 (see budget). Morgan should adjust.

## What we'll do
Governments are now writing rules that require frontier AI developers to report "serious safety incidents", such as the proposed FMIR rule (docket FMIR-2026-0042, 72-hour reporting). How those definitions are drafted decides what regulators ever learn, yet there is little systematic evidence on how the draft definitions apply to real cases.

Over four months we will build a public, carefully sourced casebook of 40–80 documented incidents involving frontier models. Two independent coders will code each case against the definitions in proposed rules: reportable, not reportable, or ambiguous. We will publish:
1. the dataset and coding scheme, under an open license;
2. inter-rater agreement statistics, as a direct measure of how ambiguous the definitions are;
3. a short report listing the specific phrases that cause ambiguity, with suggested clarifications.

## Why it matters
Incident reporting is one of the few oversight mechanisms likely to be in place before much more capable systems arrive. A definition that misses whole categories of incident, such as internal deployments, near-misses or agentic behaviour, gives regulators a false sense of coverage. This project gives rule-writers, labs and auditors concrete evidence for fixing that now, while the definitions are still being drafted.

## Why us
[Morgan to write 3–4 honest sentences: background, writing, Python, why this question.] The project needs care and consistency rather than credentials, and its outputs are fully checkable. Priya Raman, a data analyst, has committed about 5 hrs/week as second coder. We will consult [names, once they have agreed] on the coding scheme.

## Milestones
- Month 1: coding scheme piloted on 10 cases and revised after external feedback.
- Months 2–3: 40–80 cases double-coded.
- Month 4: dataset, agreement statistics and report released; results sent to the relevant docket or regulator contacts.

|---|---|
| Coder stipend (Priya, about 80 hrs at $40) | 3,200 |
| Project lead time (Morgan, about 100 hrs at a modest rate). Check with HR whether paid outside work is allowed. | 4,000 |
| Expert review honoraria (3 × $200) | 600 |
| Archiving, hosting, misc | 200 |
| **Total** | **8,000** |

# DRAFT: public comment on FMIR-2026-0042 (Frontier Model Incident Reporting)
_Status: draft. Not filed. The comment period closes **20 Nov 2026**. Comments are published with the filer's name and organisation, so this is gated on Morgan's decision and the HR constraint. I've only seen the docket summary. Morgan should read the full rule text and edit before filing._

---

I support requiring developers of frontier AI models to report serious safety incidents to the regulator within 72 hours. Timely reporting is one of the few ways a regulator can learn about problems before they become widespread. I offer five suggestions to make the rule work as intended:

1. **Define "serious safety incident" with examples.** List concrete categories, such as unauthorised access to model weights, safeguard bypasses that enable severe misuse, unexpected autonomous actions with real-world effects, and significant harm to users. Include worked examples. A vague definition will be read narrowly by those with an incentive to report less.

2. **Cover internal deployments and pre-release testing.** Some of the most important incidents may happen before public release, in internal use or testing. If the rule only covers publicly deployed models, it will miss them.

3. **Add a lighter-weight near-miss channel.** Events that could have become serious incidents are often the most informative. A low-burden, non-punitive near-miss report, possibly with a longer deadline, would greatly improve what the regulator learns.

4. **Protect people who report.** Employees and contractors who report incidents in good faith, either internally or to the regulator, should be protected from retaliation.

5. **Publish aggregate statistics.** The regulator should publish periodic anonymised summaries: counts by category, severity and time-to-report. That lets the public and researchers judge whether the system is working without exposing sensitive details.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

[Name], [Organisation, or "individual capacity"]
